verdict.reasoning: Patient describes dizziness with room spinning and unsteady walking for about 2 hours: "my room is sort of spinning and I can't walk properly..." and later confirms it has been present continuously for the past two hours.

Doctor confirms continuous symptoms for 2 hours: "So it's there now for the past two hours, you'd say?" and patient agrees. Vertigo is described as "the room is sort of spinning" and causing unsteady gait.
Patient reports "I had it a similar sort of thing about a month ago" and when asked how long it lasted: "Probably only about five, ten minutes."
Patient notes "my ears are buzzing a bit" and later "It's just a bit of a buzzy noise in my ears" during the current episode.
Patient says "No, but I am feeling very sick" when asked if she has been physically sick, and doctor labels it as "Nausea." This indicates nausea without vomiting.
Patient states "my legs and arms and everything are working fine" and doctor summarizes "So there's no weakness of your arms and legs?" without contradiction.
When asked about hearing problems, patient answers: "It's just a bit of a buzzy noise in my ears, but otherwise I can hear everything," which denies hearing loss.
Doctor asks "Any kind of ear pain or ear discharge, anything like that?" Patient responds "No, nothing."

Doctor asks about viral illness: "Did you have any kind of viral illness in the recent past. Past couple of weeks?... No cold, cough, nothing?" Patient replies "No" and "No, I've been pretty healthy."
Doctor asks "Do you have a temperature at all?" Patient answers "I don't think so," which supports denial of fever.
Patient reports past medical history: "I've had premature ovarian failure."
Patient adds "and I've taken hrt." This indicates hormone replacement therapy use.
Doctor: "It's called semitol. Yep. It's one tablet three times a day. So I'll give you about 10 days worth."
Doctor asks "Do you have any allergies at all?" Patient replies "No."
Doctor states the likely diagnosis: "the most common, you know, diagnosis we would. You're suffering from at the moment is something called labyrinthitis."
Patient says dizziness makes her feel very sick; doctor labels this as "Nausea." It is a direct clinical inference that the nausea is secondary to the vertigo.

Doctor: "So I'll send the prescription across to your pharmacy. It looks like it's the Lloyd Pharmacy on our system... It's called semitol. Yep. It's one tablet three times a day. So I'll give you about 10 days worth." This matches an electronic prescription to Lloyds pharmacy.

Doctor: "I would still like you to be seen by one of our doctors to take a look inside your ears... When. While you're with the doctors, we'd like to do your blood pressure, just examine your, you know, you know, how you're walking, and everything is." This describes in-person ear exam, BP, and gait/neurologic assessment.

Doctor advises: "if you develop any weakness of your legs or arms or, you know, a sudden headache, any of those symptoms, or you start being violently sick with it, then, you know, you would need to take yourself to A and E." This corresponds to ED for focal weakness, severe headache, or intractable vomiting.
Doctor instructs: "Just make sure you call support to book that appointment."
